title: What Sets Wages
objective: After this level you can explain what determines how much a job pays.
summary: A wage is the price of labor. Productive, well-trained workers are in more demand and in shorter supply. Dirty or dangerous jobs pay extra: a compensating differential.

cards.headline: In Adam Smith's day, a coal miner could out-earn a skilled blacksmith.
cards.body: The blacksmith had the craft. The miner had the dirt, the danger and the dark. So what really sets how much a job pays?

cards.headline: A wage is a price
cards.body: A wage is the price of labor. In the labor market, employers are the buyers, demanding workers, and workers are the sellers, supplying their time. Employers want more workers when those workers produce more, for example because they're better trained, or when customers want more of what they make. On the other side, jobs that need more education or training have fewer people able to do them.

cards.fact: In 2024, US workers with a bachelor's degree earned a median $1,543 a week.
cards.context: That compares with $930 for those with only a high school diploma, counting full-time workers aged 25 and over. Both sides of the market are at work: training can make workers more productive, which raises demand for them, and fewer people have it, which limits supply.

cards.headline: Paying for the dirt
cards.body: Back to the coal miner. Smith noticed that wages vary with the ease or hardship, and the cleanliness or dirtiness, of the work. A journeyman blacksmith seldom earned in 12 hours what a coal miner earned in 8, because mining was dirtier, more dangerous and done underground. Economists call this extra pay a compensating differential: to fill an unpleasant job, employers have to make it worth someone's while.

cards.headline: Wages: explained
learned: A wage is the price of labor
Productive, well-trained workers are in more demand
Jobs needing more training have fewer candidates
Dirty or dangerous jobs carry a compensating differential

questions.prompt: In a labor market, what is the wage?

options.label: A tax that employers pay
options.rationale: It's a price, not a tax.

options.label: The employer's profit
options.rationale: Wages are one of the costs that profit is measured after.

options.label: A gift employers choose to give
options.rationale: It's a price set in the labor market.

questions.explanation: A wage is the price of labor: employers demand workers, and workers supply their labor.

questions.prompt: Two jobs need the same skills, but one is dirty and dangerous. Which usually pays more, and why?

options.label: The safe one, since more people want it
options.rationale: Popular jobs attract plenty of workers, so they needn't pay extra.

options.label: Neither: skill alone sets the pay
options.rationale: Working conditions matter too, as Smith noticed.

options.label: The dangerous one, to attract workers
The safe one, since it is more respected
options.rationale: Hard, dirty work is what earns the extra pay here.

questions.explanation: Employers must pay extra to fill unpleasant or risky jobs: a compensating differential.

questions.prompt: A compensating differential is extra pay for an unpleasant job. In Level 48's terms, what is that extra pay?

options.label: A negative incentive, a penalty
options.rationale: Negative incentives are penalties, like fines.

options.label: A price ceiling
options.rationale: A ceiling is a legal maximum price.

options.label: A tax on dirty work
options.rationale: It's extra pay, not a tax.

questions.explanation: The extra pay rewards taking the unpleasant job, which makes it a positive incentive.
